name: Aire (Geneva)
stretch: Thairy (French border) to the Arve at Carouge
summary: The Aire was put into a straight canal in 1890–1940 to stop floods and to drain farmland; since 2002 Geneva has given parts of it a wide, natural bed again.
why: The Aire comes from the Salève in France and flows through the plain of Bernex, Confignon and Plan-les-Ouates to the Arve. Before the works it split into many channels in its upper part and made tight bends (meanders) at the foot of the Bernex–Confignon hill. From about 1860 people cut much forest on the Salève and the Mont-de-Sion. More gravel and mud came down, and the floods became worse than ever before.

Geneva wanted to protect the land from floods and to grow more food on it. The canton straightened the river from Thairy to the Lully bridge in 1890–1893. Between 1921 and 1940 it joined many small fields into larger ones (land consolidation), drained the plain and put the river into a canal down to the Arve. Later, in 1964–1970, the last part near La Praille was covered so that an industrial zone could grow.

The canal had side effects. Its bed was fixed by steps and strong dykes and lay higher than the land around it, so it was often dry in summer, and fish and plants disappeared. In 2001 Geneva passed a law to renature (make natural again) the Aire. The works of 2002–2016 kept the old canal as a historical path and dug a wide new bed next to it, where the river can move freely. The project won the Landscape Award of the Council of Europe in 2019.

stops.title: A winding river in the plain
text: In 1889 the Aire still wound through the plain below Confignon. The red dashed line shows its bends between Lully and Lancy on the map of that year.
The plain was wet and often flooded. After forest was cut on the Salève from about 1860, the river brought more gravel and the floods became stronger.

lines.name: Old winding Aire between Lully and Lancy, before 1921-1940 (traced on the 1889 map)

stops.title: The Aire becomes a canal
text: The first works came in 1890–1893, between Thairy and the Lully bridge. From 1921 to 1940 Geneva drained the plain, joined the small fields and put the river into a straight canal down to the Arve.
The blue line shows the canal (and today's bed). Compare it with the red line: the bends below Confignon are gone. The dry land became large fields for vegetables and grain.

lines.name: Old winding Aire between Lully and Lancy, before 1921-1940 (traced on the 1889 map)
The Aire today: canal of 1890-1940 and the new, wider bed of the renaturation (OpenStreetMap)

stops.title: Room for the river again
text: The canal stopped the floods, but the river was poor in life and often dry. In 2002–2016 Geneva dug a wide, shallow new bed next to the old canal, in three stages between the Certoux bridge and the Centenaire bridge.
On today's map the blue line follows the new bed; the straight canal stays beside it as a walkway. The red line still shows where the river ran before 1921.

lines.name: Old winding Aire between Lully and Lancy, before 1921-1940 (traced on the 1889 map)
The Aire today: canal of 1890-1940 and the new, wider bed of the renaturation (OpenStreetMap)

notes: Dates and stretches from the Geneva bill PL 12671 (history table). The red line is traced on the 1889 map only between Lully and Lancy, where the old bends are clear; upstream of Lully the 1889 map shows no clear course. The blue line is today's course from OpenStreetMap, which includes the renatured bed, not the 1940 canal everywhere.

name: Seymaz
stretch: Marshes of Rouelbeau and Sionnet down to the Bochet bridge
summary: From 1909 to 1924 Geneva drained the marshes of the Seymaz plain and put the stream into a straight canal of almost 5 km, to win farmland.
why: The Seymaz is a small river east of Geneva. Before 1915 its plain was covered by marshes. The marshes of Sionnet and Rouelbeau were almost one large wet area. Farmers only used it to let cattle graze and to cut litter for their stables.

In the early 20th century Geneva wanted more land for crops. The canton made plans to join small fields into larger ones and to drain the marshes. The first drains were dug in 1909–1914; the large works came in 1915–1924. The marshes were dried, the Seymaz was put into a straight canal with a very low slope, and small side streams were put into pipes under the ground.

The new fields were good, but many plants and animals of the marsh disappeared. Without the marsh, heavy rain ran off fast, and floods downstream became a problem. Since a law of 1998, Geneva has been giving the Seymaz a natural bed again near Rouelbeau and has made a new wetland in the old Sionnet marsh.

stops.title: Marshes in the Seymaz plain
text: In 1913 the Seymaz ran in bends through the wet plain near Choulex. The red areas show the marshes on the map of that year: the large Sionnet marsh and a smaller one near Rouelbeau.
The red dashed lines show the old stream through the marsh. The land was too wet for crops.

lines.name: Old winding Seymaz through the Sionnet marsh (traced on the 1913 map)

areas.name: Marais de la Touvière near Rouelbeau (marsh, 1913 map)

stops.title: A straight canal, dry fields
text: The first drains came in 1909–1914; from 1915 to 1924 the marshes were drained. The Seymaz now ran in a straight canal (blue line), and the side streams went into pipes.
On the map of 1933 the marsh symbols are gone and the plain is divided into large, regular fields.

lines.name: Old winding Seymaz through the Sionnet marsh (traced on the 1913 map)
The Seymaz today, upstream of the Bochet bridge: canal of 1915-1924 (OpenStreetMap)

areas.name: Marais de la Touvière near Rouelbeau (marsh, 1913 map)

stops.title: A wetland comes back
text: The canal could not hold heavy rain, and the plain lost most of its wildlife. A law of 1998 started the renaturation of the Seymaz.
Near Rouelbeau the stream got a natural bed again, and part of the old Sionnet marsh (red area) became a wetland once more.

The Seymaz today, upstream of the Bochet bridge: canal of 1915-1924 (OpenStreetMap)

name: Seyon (Neuchâtel)
stretch: Through the town of Neuchâtel, from Vauseyon to the lake
summary: In 1843 the town of Neuchâtel led the Seyon into a tunnel that ends 600 m further west, so its floods stopped and new streets could be built on the old river bed.
why: The Seyon comes down from the Val-de-Ruz through a gorge and once ran right through the old town of Neuchâtel to the lake. Its floods often damaged houses in the town.

The work was paid largely with the money that the merchant David de Pury left to his home town when he died in 1786. In 1843 the river was diverted (led away) into a tunnel through the hill. Its mouth moved about 600 m to the west.
The old bed in the centre was filled in. New quarters grew on it, and a street there still carries the river's name: the Rue du Seyon.

stops.title: The river leaves the town
text: Before 1843 the Seyon flowed from Vauseyon past the castle hill and through the middle of the town to the lake. The red dashed line shows this old course. It is approximate, because no map of this series is older than the work; we follow the streets that were built on the old bed.
The blue line shows the new course: a tunnel takes the river through the hill to the lake about 600 m further west.

lines.name: Old course of the Seyon through the town before 1843 (approximate, along today's Rue de l'Écluse and Rue du Seyon)
The Seyon since 1843: it leaves the town in a tunnel and reaches the lake about 600 m further west (swisstopo VECTOR25)

stops.title: A street on the old bed
text: Today the Seyon runs under the town. On the old bed there are streets and squares of the town centre, for example the Rue du Seyon.
Compare the two lines: the old mouth was near today's Place Pury, the new one is in the west, at L'Evole.

lines.name: Old course of the Seyon through the town before 1843 (approximate, along today's Rue de l'Écluse and Rue du Seyon)
The Seyon since 1843: it leaves the town in a tunnel and reaches the lake about 600 m further west (swisstopo VECTOR25)

notes: Year 1843 and the 600 m shift of the mouth from HLS 'Neuchâtel (commune)'; the canton of Neuchâtel also gives 1843. Other (tourist) pages say the tunnel works ran 1839-1844; not checked in a primary source. The red line is NOT traced on a map (no map before 1843 in the series); it follows today's streets on the old bed and is approximate. Lake shore has since been filled, so the old mouth position is approximate. The blue line is the river axis from swisstopo VECTOR25, which shows the tunnel.

name: Sense (lower course)
summary: Around 1900 the lower Sense between Thörishaus and Laupen was straightened and held in a narrow bed by dykes, to protect villages and to win farmland.
why: The Sense is the border river between the cantons of Bern and Fribourg. In its lower course it once had a wide bed of gravel with several channels, and it changed its course after big floods, for example in 1852.

People built single wooden walls along the banks from 1725 on, near villages, roads and fields. Around 1900 the river was straightened and channelled in one large correction. Between Heitibüffel and Laupen both banks got wooden walls, rolls of wire and stones, and iron posts; flood dykes further back followed in the first half of the 20th century.

The straight river flowed faster and dug its bed deeper (bed erosion). From about 1950 people built stone steps (sills) across the river to stop this; today there are 46 of them. The new land is good farmland, but the river lost its natural banks. The cantons are now studying where the Sense can get more room again (project Sense21).

stops.title: A wide gravel river
text: In 1880 the Sense between Thörishaus and Laupen ran in bends through a wide bed of gravel. The red dashed line shows the main channel on the map of that year; the red area shows the wide bed near Neuenegg and Flamatt.
After a flood the river could change its course and take away fields.

areas.name: Wide gravel bed of the Sense near Neuenegg and Flamatt (1880 map, approximate)

stops.title: A straight, narrow bed
text: Around 1900 the Sense was straightened and held between walls of wood, wire and stone. The blue line shows the new, straight bed.
Much of the old gravel bed became farmland and, later, building land for Neuenegg, Flamatt and Laupen.

stops.title: Steps against erosion
text: The fast water in the straight bed dug the river deeper. From about 1950 stone steps (sills) were built across the river below the railway viaduct at Thörishaus.
Today two thirds of the banks between the Schwarzwasser and the Saane are built up. Compare the straight blue line with the red line of 1880.

name: Aare between Thun and Bern
summary: In two corrections (1824–1859 and 1871–1892) the canton of Bern narrowed the Aare between Thun and Bern from about 400 m to about 50 m, to stop floods, win land and make the river safe for boats.
why: Between Thun and Bern the Aare once flowed in a bed up to about 400 m wide, with many channels and islands of gravel. Floods often covered the valley floor, and large parts of it could not be used.

In the 18th and 19th centuries the population grew fast. People needed more farmland and room for villages. The Aare was also an important transport route, and boats and rafts were to use it all year. For these reasons the canton of Bern corrected the river twice: from 1824 to 1859 and from 1871 to 1892. The bed was narrowed to about 50 m between dykes.

For about 100 years the corrected river worked well, and houses, roads and wells were built close to it. But the narrow, fast river dug its bed deeper, and since the Kander has flowed into Lake Thun (1714) little new gravel comes down. The groundwater sank. After the large floods of 1987 and 1999 people began to think differently about rivers. The canton then started the project 'Hochwasserschutz Aare Thun–Bern', which widens the river in places and gives it natural banks again.

stops.title: Islands and channels below Thun
text: In 1870 the Aare below Thun still split into several channels around gravel islands. The red area shows this wide bed between Thun and Uetendorf, the red dashed line the main channel.
Further downstream, towards Bern, the river had already been narrowed in the first correction of 1824–1859.

lines.name: Old main channel of the Aare below Thun, before 1871 (traced on the 1870 map)

stops.title: A straight Aare
text: The second correction (1871–1892) also narrowed the river near Thun. The blue line shows the new, straight bed between dykes.
On the map of 1895 the old channels in the red area are drying up and turning into wood and meadows.

The Aare today: straight, narrow bed of the corrections (swisstopo VECTOR25)

areas.name: Wide old gravel bed of the Aare between Thun and Uetendorf (1870 map)

stops.title: Too deep, too narrow
text: The narrow river dug itself deeper, and the groundwater in the valley sank. Today the canton of Bern has been widening the Aare in places between Thun and Bern.
Compare the narrow blue line with the wide red area of 1870.

The Aare today: straight, narrow bed of the corrections (swisstopo VECTOR25)

notes: Years 1824-1859 and 1871-1892, and the widths 400 m / 50 m, from canton of Bern documents (Oberingenieurkreis II). A slide in the 2026 presentation suggests the 1871-1892 work was mainly the stretch just below Thun and 1824-1859 the stretch down to Bern; this split is read from a sketch and not certain. Lines are drawn only for Thun–Uttigen (the stretch where the change is clear on the 1870 and 1895 maps); the stretch Uttigen–Bern was already corrected before the first map. Length c. 25 km is the Thun–Bern river distance, estimated.

name: Broye (Moudon to Lake Morat)
summary: After the flood of 1852 the Broye was straightened between Payerne and Lake Morat (1853–1856); from 1892 to 1906 the stretch from Moudon to Payerne followed, and the wet valley became farmland.
why: The Broye is a slow river with many bends. Since the Middle Ages, forest clearing had covered its plain with a thick layer of mud. The river flooded the valley often; big floods came in 1852, 1876, 1888, 1895 and 1944.

After the flood of 1852 the cantons of Vaud and Fribourg straightened and embanked the river between Payerne and Lake Morat (1853–1856). A second stage between Bressonnaz near Moudon and Pont Neuf near Payerne followed in 1892–1896 and 1898–1906, after the floods of 1876, 1888 and 1895. Smaller works came later at Villeneuve (1916–1918) and Fétigny (1924–1933).
The corrections changed the whole valley. Large wet areas became fertile fields, and the Broye valley grew into an important farming region.

stops.title: A straight canal to the lake
text: After the flood of 1852 the Broye between Payerne and Lake Morat was put into a straight bed in 1853–1856. The blue line shows this canal from Pont Neuf to Salavaux, as it appears on the map of 1870.
We cannot draw the older course here: the oldest map of this series already shows the new canal.

lines.name: The Broye canal from Payerne to Lake Morat, built 1853-1856 (swisstopo VECTOR25)

stops.title: Bends between Moudon and Payerne
text: Upstream of Payerne the river was still in its old bed in 1891. The red dashed line shows it between Moudon, Lucens and Payerne, with bends near Lucens, Curtilles and Fétigny.
Floods in 1876, 1888 and 1895 hit this part of the valley.

lines.name: Old Broye between Moudon and Payerne before 1892 (traced on the 1891 map)

stops.title: The upper valley is corrected
text: In 1892–1896 and 1898–1906 the Broye between Bressonnaz and Pont Neuf got a straighter, embanked bed (blue line). The changes are largest near Lucens and Fétigny.
The river now carried the floods away faster, and the farmers could use the valley floor.

lines.name: Old Broye between Moudon and Payerne before 1892 (traced on the 1891 map)
The Broye today between Moudon and Payerne (swisstopo VECTOR25)

stops.title: A farming valley
text: Today the Broye flows in an embanked bed along its whole lower course. The blue lines show it from Moudon to Lake Morat; the red line shows the bends of 1891.
The wide, flat fields of the valley exist because of these corrections.

lines.name: Old Broye between Moudon and Payerne before 1892 (traced on the 1891 map)
The Broye today between Moudon and Payerne (swisstopo VECTOR25)
The Broye canal from Payerne to Lake Morat, built 1853-1856 (swisstopo VECTOR25)

notes: All years from HLS 'Broye (rivière)'. The canal between the lakes of Morat and Neuchâtel belongs to the Jura water correction and is not part of this entry. No red line for 1853-1856: the first map of the series (Dufour, sheet with 1860s edition) already shows the new canal; the Dufour 1844 tiles are empty here. The winding stream east of the canal on the 1870 map is the Arbogne and was not drawn as the old Broye because this could not be confirmed. The 1891 trace is automatic and checked by eye; between Moudon and Lucens the old and new courses are almost the same at this scale.

name: Drainage of the Rhône plain (Fully–Saillon)
stretch: Rhône plain between Riddes, Saillon, Fully and Martigny
summary: After the Rhône was embanked, the low plain between Riddes and Martigny stayed wet; in 1910–1940 drainage canals and land consolidation turned it into orchards and vegetable fields.
why: The first Rhône correction (from 1863) held the river between dykes, but it did not dry the plain. Behind the dykes the water stayed in the low land. Springs such as the Sarvaz near Saillon made a large pond, the 'Grande Gouille', for months each year. The land was unhealthy and could not be farmed.

In 1873 the canton made a plan for a system of main and side canals that lead the water back into the Rhône far downstream. Most of the work came after the First World War. Between Riddes and Martigny the communes formed a consortium (a group that shares the work and the costs). Experts sorted every plot into four classes of wetness, and owners of wetter land paid more. In the plain of Saillon the fields were joined, drained and irrigated in 1914–1922.
The new land became one of the main fruit and vegetable areas of Switzerland. The old marshes, with their rare plants and birds, almost disappeared.

stops.title: Wet land behind the dykes
text: In 1905 the Rhône already ran between dykes, but the plain between Mazembroz and Saillon was still wet. The red area shows where the map of that year has marsh symbols.
Here the springs of the Sarvaz made a large pond every year.

areas.name: Wet, marshy plain between Fully and Saillon (marsh symbols on the 1905 map, approximate outline)

stops.title: Canals dry the plain
text: Between about 1910 and 1940 the communes dug drainage canals and joined the small plots into large, regular fields. The blue line shows one of these canals on the right bank, from Mazembroz past Fully to Branson.
On the map of 1950 the marsh symbols are mostly gone; straight roads and ditches divide the plain.

lines.name: Canal de la Fontaine, drainage canal on the right bank of the Rhône (swisstopo VECTOR25)

areas.name: Wet, marshy plain between Fully and Saillon (marsh symbols on the 1905 map, approximate outline)

stops.title: Orchards instead of marsh
text: Today the plain between Fully and Saillon is covered with orchards, vegetable fields and new houses. The canals still collect the water and lead it to the Rhône.
The red area shows the old wet land of 1905.

lines.name: Canal de la Fontaine, drainage canal on the right bank of the Rhône (swisstopo VECTOR25)

areas.name: Wet, marshy plain between Fully and Saillon (marsh symbols on the 1905 map, approximate outline)

notes: Period 1910-1940 from the title of the study by E. Reynard and D. Baud, 'Etude géohistorique de l'assèchement de la plaine de Riddes-Martigny (1910-1940)', Vallesia 70 (2015), cited by Thurre (Cahiers de Vallesia 33, 2020); I did not read that study itself. The 1873 plan, the Grande Gouille and the Saillon works of 1914-1922 are from Thurre; the consortium and the four wetness classes from the Valais State Archives page. The building year of the Canal de la Fontaine (blue line) is NOT confirmed; it is not visible as a clear canal on the 1905 map and is on the 1950 map, so it is shown as one example of the drainage canals. The marsh area is drawn by eye and approximate.

name: Suze (Schüss) in the Vallon de Saint-Imier
stretch: Vallon de Saint-Imier (shown: Courtelary to Cortébert)
summary: Between 1910 and 1940 a good third of the Suze (Schüss) was put into a canal; in the Vallon de Saint-Imier its bends were cut and the wet valley floor was drained.
why: The Suze (German: Schüss) flows from the Jura down the Vallon de Saint-Imier to Biel. For centuries it drove about 40 mills, saws and forges; later it powered the watch and metal industry of the valley. In the flat parts of the valley it made bends through wet meadows.

In Biel a straight arm of the river, the Schüss canal, was built from 1825 through the new quarters. Between 1910 and 1940 a good third of the river's length was canalised, to protect villages and the railway and to drain the valley floor for farming.
A plan of the canton of Bern of 1998 asks for more natural banks and better flood protection along the Suze.

stops.title: Bends below Courtelary
text: In 1905 the Suze made many small bends between Courtelary and Cortébert. The red dashed line shows this course on the map of that year.
Near Cortébert the map shows wet ground beside the river.

lines.name: Old winding Suze between Courtelary and Cortébert (traced on the 1905 map)

stops.title: A straight Suze
text: Between 1910 and 1940 the river was canalised over a good third of its length. On the map of 1946 the Suze between Courtelary and Cortébert runs in a straight bed (blue line).
The fields along the river became drier and larger.

lines.name: Old winding Suze between Courtelary and Cortébert (traced on the 1905 map)
The Suze today: canalised bed (swisstopo VECTOR25)

stops.title: The canal today
text: The Suze still runs in its straight bed of the 20th century. Compare the blue line with the red bends of 1905.
Since 1998 the canton plans more natural banks for the river.

lines.name: Old winding Suze between Courtelary and Cortébert (traced on the 1905 map)
The Suze today: canalised bed (swisstopo VECTOR25)

notes: HLS 'Schüss' gives 1910-1940 for the canalisation of 'a good third' of the river and 1825 for the Schüss canal in Biel, but does not say which stretches were canalised. That the Courtelary–Cortébert stretch belongs to the 1910-1940 works is my reading of the maps (bends in 1905, straight bed in 1946), not a written source. Only this stretch is drawn. The reasons (villages, railway, farmland) are general, not stated in the HLS article.
